reviews.text: Back to the Future, produced by Amblin Entertainment (founded by-- remember this, it's important --Steven Spielberg), is still to this day hailed as the best paradoxical media the world has ever seen. Since then, we have yearned to beat this, only to fail each time. We, the paradox community, have lost approximately 38 years of sleep merely trying to invent something worthy. Back to the Future II was less than Al Dente, and part III was more spaghetti western. After all this time, many people have given up, and more are close to it. Well, gamer nation, I am happy to say that after all these years, we can sleep. Duck Paradox is a game about a duck that is many. How Amblin Entertainment never thought of this concept may baffle you. Ladies, gentleman, and other gay creatures, it's only when you start to peel back the plastic and read between the lines that you start to realize that they did. Time travel back to the summer of '85 with me. Back to the Future just released, and to the creators' surprise and delight, it was a hit worldwide, solved world peace, cured cancer, and everything else. With their last 4 attempts were failures, the straight 388.8 million dollar turnout in the box office sealed their success. A sequel was inevitable at this point, and that came to fruition in the sunset of 1989, but that's not where we are in this story quite yet. Skip to 1986, one year after the golden movie was published. When you think '86, movies only got better from there. You had indie movies coming out like crazy; Labrynth, Little China, Top Gun, Little Shop of Horrors, Karate Kid III, Ferris Bueller, Dundee, The Fly, Flyday the 13th, Castle in the Fly, and Three Amigos. On the other hand, you had the Triple A movies critics still talk about in the present; Care Bears Movie II, Milo and Otis, of course King Kong Lives, the list goes on and on. At a crucial time of movies like this, Steven Spielberg surely wanted to make a hit, and he did make 2 movies at the time, An American Tail and The Money Pit, which both grossed between 50-100k dollars, respectively. But Spielberg wanted more. In the time between An American Tail and The Money Pit, Spielberg had a secret monster he was crafting. The idea of time travel had never left his mind, and after months of thinking, the concept finally came to him: a duck paradox. With a duck named Howard and a time machine, the world would be his. Around the beginning of November, the movie was halfway done, when a life-changing experience happened; the time machine's 1G radiation finally started to get to the duck's head. In an abrupt nightmare explosion, the duck turned into a humanoid duck. Panic rightfully ensued in the team; how could they pass this movie with this new actor? Spielberg was hesitant to pull the plug on the project, and Howard was even more hesitant to lose his chance at Hollywood fame. Using his 1G powers, he convinced Spielberg to re-shoot every scene in 7 days. After 11 days of post-production and 1 advertisement, Howard The Duck released on November 22, one day after The Money Pit. No one liked Howard The Duck. With Spielberg abandoning any responsibility for the film, the Curse of Duck Paradox has been set in place for decades now, until this very point. Euphoria has never tasted this good. Do you like projectiles that never disappear and haunt you in your paradoxical nightmares? Great! Like ducks??? I would really hope so, as this game is Ducking full of them.. One of the most promising games I tried at PAX this year. I played the demo and then turned around and bought it before I left the booth. In a hectic game like this, tight controls are paramount and they already have that on lock. Once you get a feel for it, platforming feels smooth and intuitive. Even in early access, the core game loop is already rock solid. From here forward all they need to add is more variety to levels and (potentially) more power ups to try out. I eagerly look forward to what else this game adds as it continues to develope.

I forget where I first spotted this, but I've had it on the watch-list for a while now, waiting to grab it once it finally released. Didn't know much going into it beyond a singular fixation on ducks, but having played it quite thoroughly, I can say I enjoyed my time with it! About my biggest criticism with this is the difficulty with regards to getting the endings isn't as high as I was expecting from the outset. The core of the game involves bringing Quark the duck back to the start of the level, the time machine where the game's plot originates. Exploration tools are explained clearly enough, and players are challenged to explore to find lives, duck eggs, and devices that change Quark, affecting where the portal will land them on the next level. Duck eggs give you ducklings, which can give you power boosts, regenerating shields, piercing shots, improved time-stop capabilities and so on - generally a good help to find. On top of that are shields, which are your one saving grace against the enemy; anything and everything can kill you, including your own bullets. Any shots you fire MUST hit something to dissipate, and they don't care if that something is your character. Dying restarts the level, minus one life - lose all your lives and the run ends. Simple as. But lives scattered around the level regenerate when you die; know where the lives are, and it's very easy to stay equal whilst you learn a level's layout. At that point, a run can be very difficult to lose short of exiting out of the game. Heck, one achievement ties to having 20 lives, so this isn't unexpected behaviour. The aforementioned changing of Quark lets you access different level types - the Disco and Bathroom stages. The former has you playing bat-and-ball with a glitter-ball whilst doing your best to avoid the chunkier enemies flying around, whilst the latter changes up gameplay by letting you control a duck for a short while! The aim as a duck is to bypass areas that your human self can't access, whilst bringing a time-shifted version of yourself to the same station that changed you to a duck without being hurt or dragged back to the start of the level. It's a fun little change on what's been established, though controlling the duck might be a little finicky at first. The boss fights... that [i]might[/i] be the weak point of the game, I think? One of them simply spawns guys to bother you whilst following a strict path; a second is more of a challenge on a platforming level as the ground beneath you starts to dissipate if you want to blunt its offence. The third boss works with the usual gameplay model of pitting you against an exponentially-growing horde of horrid waterfowl. Completing these fights gives you unlockable toggles for your gun, either offering traversal or greater power without being tied to the upgrades. These upgrades are key to completing the game's "Impossible" mode, which disables duckling upgrades. You get no extra defences or offences; simply reach the end of the game with your starting energy and the tools you have to unlock on each run (with the game's one kindness being to let you start with the boss drops, so you only need to get their respective component parts with the standard methods). I expected this to take me a while; [spoiler]I got it on my first run[/spoiler]. This DOES do more than just act as a challenge, so I recommend giving that a go if you grab this game. The meat of the game's challenge lies in the Survival mode. Shooting gives points, and the Kronits (energy points) the horde drops give points too, IF you're at full time-slowing juice. Points let you buy shielding, duckling eggs, and support ducks with their own firing modes, but the prices go up as you buy them from different areas. Face as many waves of weird ducks as you can before they finally overwhelm you. This is the mode that let me realise I'm not as good at this game as I thought, because my best progress still didn't reach Wave 20... So in summary: there's some good fun to this game, but the main challenge lies outside of the standard gameplay mode, which can feel like a bit of a cakewalk once you get a proper handle on the controls. [i](also I like Quark's little "I'm over here! ;_;" sounds)[/i] EDIT: Forgot to mention, the settings seem quite sparse, and the game doesn't seem to have a frame-rate cap. I don't [i]think[/i] this adversely affected my computer as Steam believed it was trying to render over two thousand frames a second, but it seems odd that the extent of this game's graphical settings are whether it was full-screen or not.
